  {

    "@type": "FAQPage",
    "mainEntity": [{
      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "What codec is best for YouTube?",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "text": "H.264 is the most common and recommended codec for uploading to YouTube due to its universal compatibility. While YouTube accepts H.265, using H.264 ensures your video can be processed quickly and viewed on all devices."
      }
    }, {
      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "Is H.265 really better than H.264?",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "text": "Yes, H.265 (HEVC) is technically superior. It offers the same visual quality as H.264 but at roughly half the file size, making it much more efficient for storage. The main trade-off is that it requires more powerful hardware to encode and decode, and it is not yet as universally supported as H.264."
      }
    }, {
      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "Is ProRes worth the extra storage space?",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "text": "For professional filmmakers, colorists, and editors, ProRes is absolutely worth the space. Its high bitrate and low compression preserve maximum image data, providing extensive flexibility in post-production for color grading and visual effects. For everyday use or direct-to-web content, it is generally overkill."
      }
    }]
  }
  </script>

      <!-- Introduction -->
      <section class="bg-white rounded-lg shadow-sm border border-slate-200 p-8 mb-12">
        <h2 class="text-2xl font-bold text-slate-900 mb-4">What Is a Video Codec and Why Does It Matter?</h2>
        <p class="text-slate-700 leading-relaxed mb-4">
          A video codec (short for coder-decoder) is a technology used to compress and decompress digital video. Think of it as a language your camera uses to shrink massive raw video files into manageable sizes.
        </p>
        <p class="text-slate-700 leading-relaxed">
          The codec you choose directly impacts three key things: **file size** (how much storage you need), **video quality**, and **editing performance**. This guide compares the three most common codecs you'll find in modern cameras: H.264, H.265, and ProRes.
        </p>
      </section>

      <!-- Quick Comparison Table -->
      <section class="bg-white rounded-lg shadow-sm border border-slate-200 p-8 mb-12">
        <h2 class="text-2xl font-bold text-slate-900 mb-6">Codec Comparison at a Glance</h2>
        <div class="overflow-x-auto" bis_skin_checked="1">
          <table class="w-full text-sm">
            <thead class="bg-slate-100 border-b border-slate-300">

                <th class="px-4 py-3 text-left font-bold text-slate-900">File Size (1 Minute)</th>
                <th class="px-4 py-3 text-left font-bold text-slate-900">Primary Use Case</th>
              </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody class="divide-y divide-slate-200">

                <td class="px-4 py-3">~100 Mbps</td>
                <td class="px-4 py-3">~750 MB</td>
                <td class="px-4 py-3">Universal Compatibility &amp; Streaming</td>
              </tr>
              <tr class="hover:bg-slate-50">
                <td class="px-4 py-3 font-medium"><span class="inline-block bg-green-100 text-green-800 px-3 py-1 rounded-full text-sm font-semibold">H.265</span></td>
                <td class="px-4 py-3">~50 Mbps</td>
                <td class="px-4 py-3">~375 MB</td>
                <td class="px-4 py-3">Efficient Storage (4K/8K)</td>
              </tr>
              <tr class="hover:bg-slate-50">
                <td class="px-4 py-3 font-medium"><span class="inline-block bg-purple-100 text-purple-800 px-3 py-1 rounded-full text-sm font-semibold">ProRes</span></td>
                <td class="px-4 py-3">400+ Mbps</td>
                <td class="px-4 py-3">3 GB+</td>
                <td class="px-4 py-3">Professional Post-Production</td>
              </tr>
            </tbody>
          </table>

      <!-- Real-World Example Section -->
      <section class="bg-indigo-50 border-t-4 border-indigo-500 rounded-b-lg p-8 mb-12 shadow-sm">
        <h3 class="text-xl font-bold text-indigo-900 mb-3 flex items-center gap-3"><i class="fas fa-calculator text-indigo-500"></i>Real-World Storage Impact</h3>
        <p class="text-indigo-800 mb-4">To understand what these bitrates mean for a project, imagine recording **1 hour of 4K 30fps video**:</p>
        <ul class="space-y-2 text-indigo-900">
          <li><strong class="font-semibold text-blue-700">H.264:</strong> Would require approximately <strong class="font-bold">45 GB</strong> of storage.</li>
          <li><strong class="font-semibold text-green-700">H.265:</strong> Would require approximately <strong class="font-bold">22.5 GB</strong> of storage (50% savings!).</li>
          <li><strong class="font-semibold text-purple-700">ProRes 422:</strong> Would require approximately <strong class="font-bold">223 GB</strong> of storage.</li>
        </ul>

      <!-- Codec Details -->
      <section class="space-y-8 mb-12">
        <!-- H.264 -->
        <div class="bg-white rounded-lg shadow-sm border border-slate-200 p-8" bis_skin_checked="1">
          <h3 class="text-2xl font-bold text-slate-900 mb-4 flex items-center gap-3">
            <span class="inline-flex items-center justify-center w-10 h-10 rounded-full bg-blue-100 text-blue-600 font-bold">1</span>
            H.264 (AVC) - The Universal Standard
          </h3>
          <div class="space-y-4 text-slate-700" bis_skin_checked="1">
            <div bis_skin_checked="1">
              <h4 class="font-bold text-slate-900 mb-2">What Is It?</h4>
              <p>For over a decade, H.264 (also known as AVC) has been the dominant video codec. It offers a great balance of quality and file size and is supported by virtually every camera, computer, smartphone, and website in existence.</p>
            </div>
            <div bis_skin_checked="1">
              <h4 class="font-bold text-slate-900 mb-2">When Should You Use H.264?</h4>
              <ul class="list-disc pl-5 space-y-1">
                <li>When your top priority is ensuring the video plays everywhere.</li>
                <li>For uploading content to YouTube, Instagram, or other social platforms.</li>
                <li>If you are using older editing software or a less powerful computer.</li>
              </ul>
            </div>
            <div class="bg-blue-50 border-l-4 border-blue-400 p-4 mt-4 rounded" bis_skin_checked="1">
              <p class="text-sm"><strong>Verdict:</strong> The safe, reliable choice for everyday recording and sharing.</p>
              <p class="text-sm mt-1"><strong>SD Card Needed:</strong> A <a href="https://sdcardchecker.com/guides/sd-card-speed-classes/" class="font-bold text-blue-600 hover:underline">V30</a> rated card is sufficient for most 4K H.264 recording.</p>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>

        <!-- H.265 -->
        <div class="bg-white rounded-lg shadow-sm border border-slate-200 p-8" bis_skin_checked="1">
          <h3 class="text-2xl font-bold text-slate-900 mb-4 flex items-center gap-3">
            <span class="inline-flex items-center justify-center w-10 h-10 rounded-full bg-green-100 text-green-600 font-bold">2</span>
            H.265 (HEVC) - The Efficient Successor
          </h3>
          <div class="space-y-4 text-slate-700" bis_skin_checked="1">
            <div bis_skin_checked="1">
              <h4 class="font-bold text-slate-900 mb-2">What Is It?</h4>
              <p>H.265, or HEVC (High Efficiency Video Coding), is the modern successor to H.264. Its main advantage is superior compression: it can deliver the same video quality at about half the bitrate, which means file sizes are 50% smaller.</p>
            </div>
            <div bis_skin_checked="1">
              <h4 class="font-bold text-slate-900 mb-2">When Should You Use H.265?</h4>
              <ul class="list-disc pl-5 space-y-1">
                <li>When you want to save storage space on your SD cards and hard drives.</li>
                <li>For recording high-resolution 4K or 8K footage.</li>
                <li>If your camera, computer, and editing software are all relatively new (made in the last ~5 years).</li>
              </ul>
            </div>
            <div class="bg-green-50 border-l-4 border-green-400 p-4 mt-4 rounded" bis_skin_checked="1">
              <p class="text-sm"><strong>Verdict:</strong> The smart choice for future-proofing and saving space, if your gear supports it.</p>
              <p class="text-sm mt-1"><strong>SD Card Needed:</strong> A <a href="https://sdcardchecker.com/guides/sd-card-speed-classes/" class="font-bold text-green-600 hover:underline">V30</a> card is still often enough, as the bitrate is lower than H.264.</p>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>

        <!-- ProRes -->
        <div class="bg-white rounded-lg shadow-sm border border-slate-200 p-8" bis_skin_checked="1">
          <h3 class="text-2xl font-bold text-slate-900 mb-4 flex items-center gap-3">
            <span class="inline-flex items-center justify-center w-10 h-10 rounded-full bg-purple-100 text-purple-600 font-bold">3</span>
            ProRes - The Professional's Choice
          </h3>
          <div class="space-y-4 text-slate-700" bis_skin_checked="1">
            <div bis_skin_checked="1">
              <h4 class="font-bold text-slate-900 mb-2">What Is It?</h4>
              <p>Developed by Apple, ProRes is a professional-grade codec designed for post-production. Unlike H.264/H.265 which prioritize small file sizes, ProRes prioritizes preserving image data. This makes files much larger but gives editors immense flexibility for color grading and effects work.</p>
            </div>
            <div bis_skin_checked="1">
              <h4 class="font-bold text-slate-900 mb-2">When Should You Use ProRes?</h4>
              <ul class="list-disc pl-5 space-y-1">
                <li>For professional film projects, commercials, or high-end client work.</li>
                <li>When you plan to do intensive color grading or VFX.</li>
                <li>If your final product needs to meet strict broadcast or cinema standards.</li>
              </ul>
            </div>
            <div class="bg-purple-50 border-l-4 border-purple-400 p-4 mt-4 rounded" bis_skin_checked="1">
              <p class="text-sm"><strong>Verdict:</strong> The ultimate choice for quality and editing flexibility, but overkill for most users due to massive file sizes.</p>
              <p class="text-sm mt-1"><strong>SD Card Needed:</strong> Requires very fast cards, typically <a href="https://sdcardchecker.com/guides/sd-card-speed-classes/" class="font-bold text-purple-600 hover:underline">V60 or V90</a>, depending on the ProRes variant.</p>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
      </section>

      <!-- Storage Calculator CTA -->
      <section class="bg-blue-600 text-white rounded-lg p-8 mb-12 text-center shadow-lg">
        <h3 class="text-2xl font-bold mb-3">Ready to Plan Your Shoot?</h3>

      <!-- FAQ Section -->
      <section class="bg-white rounded-lg shadow-sm border border-slate-200 p-8 mb-12">
        <h2 class="text-2xl font-bold text-slate-900 mb-6">Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
        <div class="space-y-4" bis_skin_checked="1">
          <details class="group">
            <summary class="flex justify-between items-center font-medium cursor-pointer list-none text-slate-800 hover:text-slate-900">
              <span>What codec is best for YouTube?</span>
              <span class="transition group-open:rotate-180">
                <i class="fas fa-chevron-down"></i>
              </span>
            </summary>
            <p class="text-slate-600 mt-3 group-open:animate-fadeIn">
              <strong>H.264 is the safest and most recommended codec for YouTube.</strong> While YouTube now accepts H.265, H.264 guarantees fast processing and flawless playback on all devices.
            </p>
          </details>
          <hr class="border-slate-200">
          <details class="group">
            <summary class="flex justify-between items-center font-medium cursor-pointer list-none text-slate-800 hover:text-slate-900">
              <span>Can I convert H.264 to H.265 to save space?</span>
              <span class="transition group-open:rotate-180">
                <i class="fas fa-chevron-down"></i>
              </span>
            </summary>
            <p class="text-slate-600 mt-3 group-open:animate-fadeIn">
              Yes, you can convert (transcode) your files, but there's a catch. Converting from one compressed format to another (like H.264 to H.265) will always result in some quality loss. It's best to record in H.265 from the start if storage is your main concern.
            </p>
          </details>
          <hr class="border-slate-200">
          <details class="group">
            <summary class="flex justify-between items-center font-medium cursor-pointer list-none text-slate-800 hover:text-slate-900">
              <span>What's the difference between bitrate and resolution?</span>
              <span class="transition group-open:rotate-180">
                <i class="fas fa-chevron-down"></i>
              </span>
            </summary>
            <p class="text-slate-600 mt-3 group-open:animate-fadeIn">
              <strong>Resolution</strong> (like 1080p or 4K) is the number of pixels in the image. <strong>Bitrate</strong> is the amount of data used to encode that image per second. You can have a 4K video with a low bitrate (poor, blocky quality) or a high bitrate (crisp, detailed quality). Higher quality demands a higher bitrate.
            </p>
          </details>
